b: Most people want to advance in their careers. That can mean going from the prep cook to the head chef, from the intern to the CEO (over a very long period), or just getting a slight raise and title bump from where you were two years ago. But whether your aspirations are expansive or just incremental, it's normal to want to feel you are being increasingly valued for what you do. That desire might be practical: Why learn and become a better worker for the same pay and recognition? Or it might be an emotional need to be seen and rewarded. Either way, it makes sense to consider how you can get to your next role.

How we prepare for the next job is not always aligned with what makes us a candidate for the next role from the employer’s side. There are things you can do differently to improve your chances for the next role or promotion. And some of it is more tactical and practical. But some of it requires a different mindset or acquiring skills unrelated to your day-to-day tasks.
How do you prepare now for your future job?

See beyond skills. Most of us start with what we know how to do, and try to keep getting better at it. If you're good at sales, you might strive to sell more, or faster, or at higher prices than colleagues. And in the early stages of your career, that's a totally appropriate mindset. In fact, it probably will help you get promoted in the early stages. Do the thing you do better than others, and you will likely see rewards in terms of bonuses and raises, and possibly a promotion. (And if you don’t, that’s a whole other conversation about your long-term relationship with that company.)

The challenge is that by early midcareer, you are likely to need to learn skills like managing people. That's not just the "downstream" people who report to you. That includes managing upstream, which means learning to not only do your job well, but do it in a way that makes your boss's life easier.

Think about it this way: When you're entry-level, your actual contribution is very low. You might not get a ton of credit for things done well. On the other hand, if you make a mistake, it’s probably low stakes. As you get more experienced, your inputs matter. People check your work less. Your contribution is noted, and your mistakes get more costly.

Recognize that promotions require people powers. As you become more senior, you will be expected not only to deliver results, but to know your manager's work style and communication preferences. Adapting to those well can become more critical than just your technical skills.

The ability to deal with people requires a certain amount of emotional strength and good mental health. There’s a reason people complain about “office politics”— and it’s not because it’s rare. Whatever term you want to use, learning to build key relationships with people you might not have a natural connection with is an important (and difficult) skill to learn.

Visualize a role. Another challenge is visualizing the next role in your mind. People understandably get very practical — they focus on a title they want or a certain salary. But they don't picture the whole role. Imagine a job description. It's more than title and compensation. What are the responsibilities? What prior experience is most valuable? Think about what that role entails and what gaps you have now.

A lot of people suffer from imposter syndrome, both in their efforts to be promoted, and even if (especially if!) they actually get the job. Imagine yourself in the role, and practice "acting as if" (yes, it's a real thing to visualize and act as if you are doing the thing you want to do well). It's like rehearsing before a big performance. You won't be less nervous (apparently even Adele gets horrible stage fright – nerves are not about ability), but what it does is let your competence make up for confidence. You can't make yourself "feel" like you're ready for a job. What you can do is practice communication, contributions, and other behaviors necessary for that role. Ideally, by the time the promotion comes, you'll be capable of a lot of the demands, even if you're not yet confident.

Ask yourself why you want the next role. (Hint: money is not enough.) This one can be the toughest because people take for granted that they ought to "want" to advance. Even though it's probably true that many people want to keep getting bigger roles, some people don't. Yes, really — and it's ok if you are one of those people. I once advised a client who had a short list of people they thought would be great to take over the top levels of the company, literally potential C-suite team members, and never thought to ask if they wanted the jobs. I've also worked with someone who knew they didn't want it and was happy to communicate that (they had a parent who had been in the top position, saw what "success" looked like up close, and turned away).
Make sure the next role is an audition you want

Of course, all of this assumes you’ve stopped and considered if the next role is what you want. Money isn’t nothing — there’s a point at which more money is a real factor and sufficient to keep you motivated. But at some point, many people have enough experience that they could do multiple different things that would earn enough. If all goes well, money stops being the only motivator. So make sure that advancing to the next role is worth it to you in ways that are positive and related to this specific role. For example, believing in the product or service you're working on, enjoying the people you work with, and working with a company whose ethics align with yours are all legitimate and durable motivations. This is what makes the work worthwhile in the long run. Before you commit to the hard work of getting the role, make sure the true payoff is there.
